name: Mucuna pruriens (velvet bean)
short: Contains levodopa. In Parkinson's disease a review links overuse and unsupervised use to dyskinesia, dopamine dysregulation and psychiatric problems. Raw seeds: vomiting, hallucinations (case report).
text: Mucuna pruriens seeds contain levodopa, the standard medicine for Parkinson's disease symptoms, and a 2026 review cautions that, despite its natural origin, Mucuna is a potent dopaminergic therapy requiring the same caution as levodopa-based medicines; the review states that overuse and unsupervised self-medication have been associated with dyskinesia, dopamine dysregulation syndrome and psychiatric complications, that cases of toxicity have followed improper seed preparation, and that long-term safety data are still scarce. A case report describes a 58-year-old woman who ate 5 raw seeds and, about 40 minutes later, developed nausea, vomiting and abundant diarrhoea followed by confusion, hallucinations and amnesia. Another case report describes dopamine dysregulation syndrome in a patient with Parkinson's disease who took self-directed Mucuna pruriens alongside prescribed carbidopa/levodopa; taking it together with levodopa medicines is the only interaction named in the cited sources. The trial evidence comparing Mucuna with levodopa in Parkinson's disease is limited: a systematic review of 5 clinical trials (108 participants; three rated low quality) reported fewer adverse events and no dyskinesia with Mucuna, but called the current clinical evidence limited and said further high-quality trials are needed to confirm its efficacy and safety, and a randomised crossover study in 18 patients with advanced Parkinson's disease, which tested only single doses, found fewer dyskinesias and adverse events than with levodopa/benserazide and no difference in cardiovascular response. The 2026 review says Mucuna's use should remain restricted to clinical trials or to treatment plans led by a neurologist until there is stronger evidence of its long-term safety and efficacy.
